title: The order of rate increases matters when optimistic investors are leveraged
summary: Jonathan Goldberg and David López-Salido ask what happens when a central bank tries to restrain a speculative boom after investors have already borrowed against high asset valuations. In their model, a surprise that sharply lowers current prices can damage the very balance sheets that would otherwise absorb risk in a downturn. The policy that best manages that trade-off announces a firmer expected rate path while postponing much of the restraint. Its success depends on the path of asset prices and on who bears a fall in their value. This Banco de España working paper is calibrated to US business-cycle evidence and studies a low-interest-rate environment. The exercise concerns the interaction of leverage and limited room to ease during a bust.

Investors disagree about the prospects for risky assets. Optimists borrow from more pessimistic investors and buy more of the risky claims. This makes the optimists’ share of aggregate wealth especially sensitive to asset prices. A reversal in risk perceptions can send those prices down even without a fall in current productivity. The loss of wealth curtails spending, and a policy rate at the zero lower bound prevents the central bank from fully offsetting the hit to demand. The investors most inclined to hold risky assets are also the ones most exposed to a mark-to-market loss.

The authors distinguish two changes in wealth that occur at different times. Once investors have adjusted to a lower valuation in the boom, a subsequent bust involves a smaller price fall and less destruction of optimists’ wealth. That is the insurance gained from leaning against the boom. But getting from today’s high valuation to the lower one can itself produce an immediate loss. Leveraged investors hold fewer resources after that initial surprise, leaving them less able to support prices and demand when sentiment eventually deteriorates. A comparison that imposes a lower pre-bust valuation while holding the distribution of wealth fixed captures the insurance benefit and omits the cost of announcing the policy.

The preferred transition preserves more of the optimists’ wealth on announcement, then allows valuations to decline gradually if speculation continues. Figure 5 shows how this changes the timing of restraint. The lower-left panel plots average expected policy rates over different horizons. Five years after the announcement, if the boom persists, short-horizon rates have risen most and the curve has flattened. The lower-right panel instead holds the boom state fixed and plots forward rates. On announcement these exceed conventional-policy forwards except at very short horizons. The authors’ supplemental Figure IA.5 allows a state change and retains the higher forwards beyond the initial period. An observed bond yield also includes compensation for duration risk.

The quantitative exercise uses returns across US business cycles and the sensitivity of intermediary capital to asset prices to discipline the role of leverage. Table 1 sets the benchmark leverage limit at 4.3. The authors also consider a separate calibration based on international asset returns around the global financial crisis. The conventional policy stabilises output during the boom and leaves optimists exposed to the subsequent price correction. A simple, unexpected restriction that drives asset prices down immediately can lower welfare. Phasing the tightening in sacrifices some immediate insurance and depresses boom-time output, yet in the calibration that cost is small relative to the improvement in the subsequent downturn. Those comparisons depend on the assumed inability to cut rates sufficiently after a bust.

Two extensions delimit what can be inferred. In one, a policy that damages optimists’ wealth at announcement is assumed to increase the arrival rate of a bust, while gradual restraint lowers it. The probability response is an assumption. Its size would need to be estimated from actual episodes. Allowing gradual restraint to extend the expected life of the boom can increase its welfare benefits but also makes a protracted period of below-potential output more costly. In another extension some speculative booms end well. The authors show that a particular phased policy can reproduce the welfare benefits of a small tightening of the leverage constraint. They leave the full optimal rate path for that mixed case open. The result most relevant to event research is the distinction between raising expected future rates and triggering an abrupt loss for the institutions currently bearing the risk.

questions.question: Can announcement damage be identified separately from the expected path of rates?
questions.detail: Separate changes in the next-meeting rate from changes in forward rates around announcements. Match these surprises to intermediary equity returns, funding spreads and pre-announcement leverage from regulatory balance sheets. The paper predicts larger losses when the investors who hold the risk enter the announcement with thin capital. Mark the release times of economic data and earnings surprises to test whether they explain the same price move.

questions.question: Does a steeper government yield curve actually represent backloaded tightening?
questions.detail: Compare government yields with meeting-dated overnight indexed swaps or short-rate futures, then estimate how much of the remaining move reflects term premia or changed recession odds. Primary-dealer surveys can identify episodes where respondents expected the expansion to persist. Figure 5 and supplemental Figure IA.5 give two distinct empirical targets. Track the conditional and unconditional paths separately, and check whether near-term rates subsequently rise more as a boom ages.

questions.question: How much does proximity to a future rate floor change the welfare trade-off?
questions.detail: Measure the pre-announcement probability of reaching the lower bound using interest-rate options and the distribution of surveyed rate forecasts. Compare highly leveraged episodes with similar current short rates but different room to ease after a bust. Follow realised credit and demand after the downturn and check whether the initial distribution of intermediary capital explains their response. Separate this policy-space test from estimates of whether restraint changes the probability of a bust.
